questions.question: What two operations must a vector space be equipped with?
options: Vector addition and multiplication of two vectors.
Scalar multiplication and the dot product.
Vector addition and a length for each vector.

questions.question: What does closure under addition mean?
options: If $x\in V$, then $x$ must be a scalar.

questions.question: What does closure under scalar multiplication mean?
options: Only the scalar $1$ may be used.
If $\alpha\in\mathbb{F}$ and $x\in V$, then $\alpha x\in V$.
Every scalar must be a vector.

questions.question: Why is $\mathbb{R}^n$ the standard example of a vector space?
options: It has coordinatewise addition and real scalar multiplication.
It has coordinatewise addition and coordinatewise multiplication.
Its vectors have lengths and angles, which define a vector space.
Every vector space is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some $n$.

questions.question: Which object must exist so that every $x\in V$ satisfies $x+\boldsymbol0=x$?
Do the polynomials of degree at most $2$ form a vector space under the usual addition and scalar multiplication?
options: No; they have no zero element
No; they are not closed under addition

questions.question: Which set is a vector space under ordinary operations?
options: The positive real numbers with ordinary vector addition as coordinates.

questions.question: Which vector-space axiom fails for $\{(x,y)\colon x+y=1\}$ under ordinary operations?
options: Addition on it is not commutative.
The scalar identity $1x=x$ fails on it.
It does not contain the zero vector.
It is a line, and no line can be a vector space.

questions.question: The set of all $m\times n$ real matrices is a vector space under which operations?
options: Matrix multiplication and real scalar multiplication.
Matrix addition and multiplication by other matrices.
Matrix addition and real scalar multiplication.

questions.question: In a vector space, what is $0\cdot v$ (the zero scalar times any vector $v$)?
Why is a vector space called the basic setting for linear algebra?
options: Its vectors can be multiplied and divided like numbers.
It is any set of arrows with a length and a direction.
Its elements are always finite lists of real numbers.
It is where addition, scaling, spans and bases live.

questions.question: What does the cancellation law say in a vector space?
Why is the scalar field part of the definition of a vector space?
options: It specifies which scalars may multiply vectors.
It determines only the notation, not the operations.

questions.question: If $V$ is a vector space and $x\in V$, what must $-x$ satisfy?
options: $-x$ is a scalar, not a vector.

questions.question: What is a subset of a vector space $V$ called if it is itself a vector space under the same operations?
Which statement uses distributivity over vector addition?
Why is checking only closure under addition not enough to prove a set is a vector space?
options: Closure must also hold for multiplying two vectors together.
Closure under addition also gives closure under scalar multiplication.
Scalar closure, zero, inverses and the other axioms must hold too.
Only the zero vector must also be checked; the rest is automatic.

questions.question: A bare set of vectors lacks operations. Which additional structure turns it into a vector space?
options: A length for each vector and an angle between vectors.
A chosen basis and coordinates for every vector.
Addition and scalar multiplication, with no further rules.
Addition and scalar multiplication obeying the axioms.

questions.question: A proposed space contains $x$ but not $-x$. Which axiom is violated?
If $u,v\in V$ and $\alpha,\beta$ are scalars, must $\alpha u+\beta v\in V$?
